problem: The stated order for making the mould skips the cope completely. It goes: drag flask on board, pattern, ram, draw pattern, cut gates, then 'the cope is closed on the drag'. Nothing ever says the cope was rammed, so a student reads the cope as a ready-made cover. The sprue is also never formed, although the text says metal enters through a vertical sprue in the cope. The figure repeats the same gap: it jumps from 'Gating cut' to 'Cope closed'.
fix: Give both halves. Drag: place the drag flask on a board, place the pattern, ram the sand, draw the pattern, cut the runner and gate. Cope: turn the drag over, place the cope flask and the other half of the pattern with a sprue pin, ram the sand, withdraw the sprue pin (which leaves the sprue), lift the cope and set it on the drag with locating pins. Add the cope-ramming step to the figure before 'Cope closed'.

problem: 'A sand mould is a refractory sand shape: it stays strong when hot' defines refractoriness wrongly. Refractoriness is resistance to fusing or softening at the temperature of the molten metal; it does not mean the mould keeps its strength when hot. The chapter's own table gives the correct meaning, so the two statements clash.
fix: Write: 'A sand mould is a refractory sand shape: it does not fuse or soften at the temperature of the molten metal.' Drop 'stays strong when hot'.

problem: 'some syllabi call it foundry sand' is misleading. Foundry sand is the general name for any sand a foundry uses; green sand is one kind of it (moist, clay-bonded sand). The sentence reads as if the two names mean the same thing.
fix: Write: 'Green sand is one kind of foundry sand; the general name foundry sand covers green sand, dry sand and loam.'
